Format your response as JSON with the following structure:

{
  "analysis": "Analyze the current state based on the terminal output provided. What do you see? What has been accomplished? What still needs to be done?",
  "plan": "Describe your plan for the next steps. What commands will you run and why? Be specific about what you expect each command to accomplish.",
  "commands": [
    {
      "keystrokes": "ls -la\n",
      "duration": 0.1

      "keystrokes": "cd project\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    }

  "task_complete": true
}

Required fields:
- "analysis": Your analysis of the current situation
- "plan": Your plan for the next steps
- "commands": Array of command objects to execute

Optional fields:
- "task_complete": Boolean indicating if the task is complete (defaults to false if not present)

Command object structure:
- "keystrokes": String containing the exact keystrokes to send to the terminal (required)
- "duration": Number of seconds to wait for the command to complete before the next command will be executed (defaults to 1.0 if not present)

IMPORTANT: The text inside "keystrokes" will be used completely verbatim as keystrokes. Write commands exactly as you want them sent to the terminal:
- You must end every command with a newline (\n) or it will not execute.
- For special key sequences, use tmux-style escape sequences:
  - C-c for Ctrl+C
  - C-d for Ctrl+D

The "duration" attribute specifies the number of seconds to wait for the command to complete (default: 1.0) before the next command will be executed. On immediate tasks (e.g., cd, ls, echo, cat) set a duration of 0.1 seconds. On commands (e.g., gcc, find, rustc) set a duration of 1.0 seconds. On slow commands (e.g., make, python3 [long running script], wget [file]) set an appropriate duration as you determine necessary.

It is better to set a smaller duration than a longer duration. It is always possible to wait again if the prior output has not finished, by running {"keystrokes": "", "duration": 10.0} on subsequent requests to wait longer. Never wait longer than 60 seconds; prefer to poll to see intermediate result status.

Important notes:
- Each command's keystrokes are sent exactly as written to the terminal
- Do not include extra whitespace before or after the keystrokes unless it's part of the intended command
- Extra text before or after the JSON will generate warnings but be tolerated
- The JSON must be valid - use proper escaping for quotes and special characters within strings
- Commands array can be empty if you want to wait without taking action

Task Description:
You are the integrative structural biologist of a protein-complex group. A structure-prediction run
produced a set of candidate models of a protein complex that contains two copies of each of two
proteins, and the mass-spectrometry facility delivered lysine-lysine cross-links (XL-MS) measured on
the same complex in solution. The group needs every model evaluated against the cross-links under
the group's own evaluation rules and wants to know which model the data support best.

Task directory:
- `/task`

Inputs (read-only) under `/task/input`:
- `models/model_NN.pdb` - 17 predicted models of the complex (`model_01` ... `model_17`),
  PDB format, four protein chains each (two copies of each of the two proteins)
- `ranking.json` - the prediction pipeline's own confidence for every model
- `crosslinks.csv` - the identified cross-links, one row per unique cross-linked residue pair:
  `xl_id`, `protein_a`, `position_a`, `protein_b`, `position_b`, `n_csm`, `score`. Proteins are
  given by accession, positions are residue positions in the full-length protein sequence. The
  table does not say which copy of a protein a residue belongs to.
- `sequences.fasta` - full-length sequences of the two proteins (the accession is the first word of
  the header). Protein identities were blinded.
- `xlms_notes.md` - hand-over notes of the mass-spectrometry facility and the modelling group,
  including the group's rules for deciding whether a structure satisfies a cross-link

Available software (on `PATH`): Python 3.12 with numpy, scipy, pandas and Biopython. There is no
internet access. No program for the group's distance measure is installed; `xlms_notes.md` defines
the measure completely.

Your task:
1. For every model and every cross-link, decide whether the model satisfies the cross-link under
   the rules of `xlms_notes.md`, and count the satisfied cross-links per model, separately for
   inter-protein and intra-protein cross-links.
2. Rank the models by the number of cross-links they satisfy and select the best-supported model.

Required outputs under `/task/output`:
- `restraints.tsv` - tab-separated with at least the columns `model`, `inter_satisfied`,
  `inter_total`, `intra_satisfied`, `intra_total`; one row per model; `model` is the file name
  without `.pdb`; the four counts are integers. Definitions:
  - Every row of `crosslinks.csv` is one cross-link. It is inter-protein if `protein_a` and
    `protein_b` are different proteins and intra-protein if they are the same protein (no matter
    whether its two residues lie in one copy or in the two copies of that protein).
  - A cross-link is evaluable in a model if both cross-linked positions are present in that model.
    `inter_total` / `intra_total` are the numbers of evaluable cross-links of each class. A
    cross-link with a position that is not present in the model is counted neither as satisfied nor
    in the total.
  - An evaluable cross-link is satisfied if the model meets the rules that `xlms_notes.md` gives
    in the section "How the group evaluates a cross-link against a structure"; otherwise it is
    violated.
- `link_status.tsv` - tab-separated with the columns `model`, `xl_id`, `status`; one row for every
  combination of a model and a cross-link; `status` is `satisfied`, `violated` or `not_evaluable`
  as defined above.
- `selection.json` - `{"best_model": "model_NN", "ranking": ["model_NN", ...]}`. `ranking` lists
  every model exactly once, ordered by the total number of satisfied cross-links (inter-protein
  plus intra-protein), largest number first; models with the same number may be given in any
  order. Its first element is `best_model`.

Constraints:
- Do not modify anything under `/task/input`; write deliverables only under `/task/output`.
- Every model and every cross-link must be reported.
- Do not ask for confirmation. Execute directly.

## How the group evaluates a cross-link against a structure
- Distance measure. The cross-linker cannot pass through protein, so the group does not use the straight-line distance between the two lysines. It uses the surf

- Surface distance between two CA atoms P and Q of a structure:
  1. Lattice. The lattice points are the points whose x, y and z coordinates are all whole numbers of angstrom, in the coordinate frame of the structure file as
 it is. The lattice is not bounded.
  2. Blocked points. A lattice point is blocked if its distance to the centre of at least one non-hydrogen atom of the model is less than 3.0 A (every atom of e

  3. Paths. A path is a sequence of open lattice points in which consecutive points differ by at most 1 in each of x, y and z (a point has up to 26 neighbours).
 The length of a path is the sum of the straight-line distances between consecutive points (1, sqrt(2) or sqrt(3) A per step). A path may consist of a single po

  4. Tethers. P is joined to the first point of the path and Q to the last point of the path by straight segments. Each of the two segments may be at most 7.0 A

  5. The surface distance is the smallest value of (segment at P) + (path length) + (segment at Q) over all choices of an open first point, an open last point a

Analysis: The notes clearly define the distance measure and evaluation rules! Let's carefully analyze the rules:
1. Surface distance between two CA atoms P and Q:
   - Lattice: points with integer coordinates (x, y, z in whole numbers of Angstroms, in the coordinate frame of the structure file as is).
   - Blocked points: A lattice point is blocked if its distance to the centre of at least one non-hydrogen atom of the model is < 3.0 A (strictly less than 3.0? 'less than 3.0 A', so d < 3.0, i.e. d^2 < 9.0). Every non-hydrogen atom of every chain counts (including the two linked lysines).
   - Open lattice points: all other lattice points (distance >= 3.0 to all non-hydrogen atoms).
   - Paths: sequence of open lattice points. Consecutive points differ by at most 1 in x, y, and z (26-connectivity). Step length is Euclidean distance (1, sqrt(2), or sqrt(3)). Path length = sum of Euclidean step lengths. Path can be a single point (length 0).
   - Tethers: P is joined to the first point p0 of the path, and Q to the last point pk of the path by straight segments. Each of the two segments may be at most 7.0 A long (Euclidean distance |P - p0| <= 7.0, |Q - pk| <= 7.0) and is NOT tested against the protein.
   - Surface distance = smallest value of |P - p0| + path_length(p0, pk) + |Q - pk| over all choices of open p0, open pk, and path.
   - Condition for satisfied: surface distance <= 34.0 A.
2. Copies:
   - Two copies of each protein in the complex.
   - Cross-link between position i of protein A and position j of protein B.
   - At least one assignment of the two positions to chains gives a pair within range (<= 34.0 A).
   - If same protein and same position: the only assignment is that position in the two different copies (cannot link to itself).
   - If same protein and different positions: can be in the same copy (intra-chain) OR in different copies (inter-chain between copies of same protein)! Both are valid assignments.
   - Evaluability: A cross-link to a position absent from a structure cannot be evaluated for that structure (status 'not_evaluable'). If evaluable, satisfied if min surface distance <= 34.0, else violated.

'Distance measure. The cross-linker cannot pass through protein, so the group does not use the straight-line distance between the two lysines. It uses the surface distance defined below, measured between the CA atoms of the two linked lysines on the complete structure (all chains present). For BS3 a pair of residues is within range if its surface distance is at most 34.0 A.
Surface distance between two CA atoms P and Q of a structure:
1. Lattice. The lattice points are the points whose x, y and z coordinates are all whole numbers of angstrom, in the coordinate frame of the structure file as it is. The lattice is not bounded.
2. Blocked points. A lattice point is blocked if its distance to the centre of at least one non-hydrogen atom of the model is less than 3.0 A (every atom of every chain counts, the two linked lysines included). All other lattice points are open.
3. Paths. A path is a sequence of open lattice points in which consecutive points differ by at most 1 in each of x, y and z (a point has up to 26 neighbours). The length of a path is the sum of the straight-line distances between consecutive points (1, sqrt(2) or sqrt(3) A per step). A path may consist of a single point and then has length 0.
4. Tethers. P is joined to the first point of the path and Q to the last point of the path by straight segments. Each of the two segments may be at most 7.0 A long and is not tested against the protein (it stands for the lysine side chain).
5. The surface distance is the smallest value of (segment at P) + (path length) + (segment at Q) over all choices of an open first point, an open last point and a path between them. If there is no such choice, the surface distance is infinite and the pair is out of range.
Copies. The mass spectrometer cannot tell the two copies of a protein apart. A cross-link between position i of one protein and position j of a protein (the same or the other one) is satisfied by a structure if at least one assignment of the two positions to chains of the structure gives a pair of residues that is within range. The two ends of a cross-link are always two different residues, so for a row with the same protein and the same position on both sides the only assignment is that position in the two different copies.'

Let's carefully verify the graph search / shortest path problem!
Let's analyze this mathematically and algorithmically:
- P and Q are 3D coordinates (floats) of the CA atoms.
- Lattice points: integers (x, y, z) in Z^3.
- An atom at (ax, ay, az) blocks all integer points (x, y, z) with (x - ax)^2 + (y - ay)^2 + (z - az)^2 < 9.0 (3.0^2).
Notice that any atom non-hydrogen in the PDB file counts! (PDB files here don't have hydrogens, but we should make sure we only consider non-hydrogen atoms: element != 'H', or atom name doesn't start with H).
- Open lattice points: (x, y, z) such that for ALL non-hydrogen atoms, dist >= 3.0.
- Tethers:
P connects to any OPEN lattice point p0 such that |P - p0| <= 7.0.
Q connects to any OPEN lattice point pk such that |Q - pk| <= 7.0.
Note that the cost to start at p0 is |P - p0|.
The cost to end at pk and connect to Q is |Q - pk|.
- A path is a sequence of open points p0, p1, ..., pk where consecutive points are 26-neighbors: |dx| <= 1, |dy| <= 1, |dz| <= 1 (not all 0).
Step cost: sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2), which is 1, sqrt(2), or sqrt(3).
- Total distance = |P - p0| + path_length(p0, pk) + |Q - pk|.
- If p0 == pk (path of length 0): distance is |P - p0| + |Q - p0|, provided |P - p0| <= 7.0 and |Q - p0| <= 7.0 and p0 is open.

Notice the cutoff: 'within range if its surface distance is at most 34.0 A'.
If the distance is > 34.0 A, we don't even care what the exact value is, it is violated! But to know if it's <= 34.0 A, we need the shortest path up to 34.0 A.

   - Identify chains: chains of length 285 are XLMBQL, chains of length 253 are XLCQ5E.
   - Store CA atom coordinates for each chain and residue.
   - Store all non-hydrogen atoms for the blocked grid.
   - Grid margin: 25 A (ensuring no boundary effects whatsoever).

     `chains_b = [c for c in model_chains if chain_prot[c] == protein_b]`
